title: I Hid a Runaway Pig for 40 Days to Save Her From the Slaughterhouse, Then My Heart Gave Out and She Ran Into the Road
fb_text:
For 40 mornings, I hid a runaway pig in my barn so she wouldn't go to the slaughterhouse. My neighbor found out. "That's my pig, old man. Bacon by Sunday, and you'll pay for every day you hid her." On the 41st morning, I collapsed with a heart attack on my kitchen floor. And the pig ran into the road.

My name is Warren. I'm seventy years old. I'm a retired mail carrier, and I live alone on a few acres outside Lancaster, Pennsylvania.

My wife passed away four years ago. Since then, it's just been me and the quiet. I have a bad heart. Two stents. A bottle of nitroglycerin pills in my pocket at all times.

My neighbor is Burt. He raises pigs for a meat company. Two hundred of them, in long metal barns that smell for a mile.

In September, one of Burt's trucks was driving down our road toward the processing plant. It hit a pothole. The back gate rattled open.

One pig jumped out.

She was small for a pig. Pink with black spots. One ear flopped over. She ran straight into the cornfield behind my house and vanished.

The truck never stopped.

That night, I heard something rooting around by my garbage cans. I went out with a flashlight.

There she was. Shaking. Scared. A cut on her leg from the jump.

She looked up at me with small, smart eyes.

I don't know why I did what I did. I had eaten bacon my whole life.

But I opened the door of my empty barn and set down a bucket of water and some apples.

She walked right in.

I named her Dolly.

Every morning after that, I fed her. Apples. Corn. Leftover bread. I cleaned the cut on her leg. I sat on an overturned bucket and talked to her about my wife, about the weather, about nothing at all.

She followed me around like a dog. She learned her name in three days. She learned to sit for an apple in a week. Every morning when I walked into the barn, she squealed and spun in a circle.

She was the best company I'd had in four years.

On the fortieth day, Burt showed up at my door.

He's a big man in his fifties. Red face. Always angry.

"Warren," he said, "one of my drivers saw a spotted pig in your yard. I'm missing one from the September load."

I didn't lie to him.

"She jumped off your truck. She was hurt. I took care of her."

"That's my pig. I'm taking her."

"Burt, I'll buy her from you. What's she worth?"

He laughed.

"She's not for sale. She's property. And you've been hiding stolen property for over a month." He jabbed a finger at my chest. "I'm coming back Sunday with my trailer. That pig goes to the plant. Bacon by Sunday. And if you give me any trouble, I'll call the sheriff and have you charged with theft. You'll pay me for every day you hid her."

Then he walked off my porch.

That night, I sat in the barn with Dolly for a long time. She rested her head in my lap.

I didn't sleep. I didn't argue anymore. I just told her, very quietly, "Okay. We'll figure it out."

The next morning was day forty-one.

I was standing in my kitchen making coffee when a pain hit my chest like a hammer.

I couldn't breathe. My left arm went numb. The coffee pot slipped from my hand and shattered on the floor.

I reached for the pill bottle in my pocket. My fingers wouldn't work. It fell and rolled under the stove.

I went down next to it.

My phone was on the kitchen table. Six feet away. It might as well have been six miles.

I tried to crawl. I couldn't.

I don't know how long I lay there. Ten minutes. Maybe more.

Then I heard a loud squeal at the back door.

Dolly.

She had pushed open the barn door. She was standing outside the kitchen, looking at me through the screen.

She squealed again. Then she shoved the screen door open with her nose and trotted over to me. She sniffed my face. She nudged my cheek.

"Good girl," I whispered. "Go. Get help."

I don't know if she understood.

But she turned around and ran out the door.

Straight down my driveway.

And out onto the road.

The last thing I saw before everything went dark was a little spotted pig running toward the highway, where the cars go sixty miles an hour.

For 40 mornings, Warren hid a runaway pig in his barn so she would never reach the slaughterhouse. On the 41st morning, his heart nearly gave out, and the pig he had saved ran into the road.

A Quiet Life Outside Lancaster

Warren is seventy, a retired mail carrier living alone on a few acres outside Lancaster, Pennsylvania. His wife died four years ago, and since then it had been just him and the quiet. He has a bad heart, two stents, and a bottle of nitroglycerin pills that never leaves his pocket.

His neighbor, Burt, raises two hundred pigs for a meat company in long metal barns that smell for a mile.

The Pig Who Jumped

One September day, a truck from Burt's farm hit a pothole on the way to the processing plant. The back gate rattled open, and one small pig jumped out. She was pink with black spots, and one of her ears flopped over. She disappeared into the cornfield behind Warren's house. The truck never stopped.

That night, Warren heard something rooting by his garbage cans. He went out with a flashlight and found her shaking, scared, with a cut on her leg. She looked up at him with small, smart eyes.

"I don't know why I did it," he says. "I'd eaten bacon my whole life."

He opened the door of his empty barn and set down water and apples. She walked right in. He named her Dolly.

Every morning he fed her, cleaned her wound, and sat on an overturned bucket telling her about his wife and the weather. She learned her name in three days and how to sit for an apple in a week. Each morning she squealed and spun in circles when he opened the barn door. She was the best company he'd had in four years.

Bacon by Sunday

On the fortieth day, Burt showed up on the porch, red-faced and angry. A driver had spotted a pig in Warren's yard.

Warren didn't lie. He offered to buy her. Burt laughed. "She's property," he said. "Bacon by Sunday. And you'll pay me for every day you hid her." He threatened to call the sheriff and charge Warren with theft.

That night Warren sat in the barn while Dolly rested her head in his lap. "Okay," he told her quietly. "We'll figure it out."

Day Forty-One

The next morning, while he was making coffee, a pain hit his chest like a hammer. His left arm went numb. The coffee pot shattered on the floor. The pill bottle slipped from his fingers and rolled under the stove, and Warren went down beside it. His phone sat on the table, six feet away, and he could not reach it.

Then he heard a squeal at the back door. Dolly had pushed open the barn door. She nosed through the screen, trotted to him, and nudged his cheek.

"Good girl," he whispered. "Go. Get help."

She turned and ran down the driveway and onto the road. The last thing Warren saw was a small spotted pig heading toward the highway, where the cars go sixty miles an hour.

What Happened Next

A woman named Carol was driving to work when a spotted pig burst out in front of her car. She slammed the brakes and stopped inches away. Instead of running off, the pig stood in the middle of the road, squealing, and would not move.

When Carol stepped out, the pig ran a few steps up Warren's driveway, then turned and looked back at her. She did it again. And again.

Carol followed. Through the open kitchen door she saw Warren on the floor, gray and barely breathing. She called 911 and stayed beside him until the ambulance arrived. The paramedics later told him the delay of even a few more minutes might have been fatal.

Warren woke in the hospital with a new stent and a nurse telling him he was lucky. He knew it was more than luck.

Burt's Visit

On his third day there, the door opened and Burt walked in, hat in his hands. Word had traveled fast. The paramedics had told the whole road about the pig that stopped traffic.

Burt stood quiet for a long moment. "My dad died of a heart attack on his kitchen floor," he finally said. "Nobody found him for a day." He cleared his throat. "That pig's not going to any plant. Consider her yours. No charge."

Warren came home a few weeks later. Dolly was waiting at the fence, squealing and spinning in circles. Carol had been feeding her apples every day.

These days, Dolly has the run of the yard and a warm spot by the back door. Warren keeps his phone in his pocket, and his pills in two places. On quiet mornings, he sits on the overturned bucket, and the quiet doesn't feel so empty anymore.
